messages.content: Can you retrieve the weather forecast for White Plains for next week with temperatures in Celsius?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

We need to call the function requests_get with appropriate params. The user wants forecast for next week for White Plains. We need to get coordinates for White Plains. White Plains is a city in New York, USA. Coordinates approx 41.0535°N, -73.7629°W. So latitude=41.0535, longitude=-73.7629. They want temperatures in Celsius. The Open-Meteo API returns temperature units based on parameter "temperature_unit". By default it's celsius? Actually default is celsius. But we can specify "temperature_unit=celsius". Also we might want daily forecast for next week. The API supports daily parameters like "daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min". And "forecast_days=7"? Actually there's "forecast_days" param. Let's check typical usage: For daily forecast, you can set "daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min" and "forecast_days=7". Or "start_date" and "end_date". We'll just use "forecast_days=7". Also "timezone=auto" to get local timezone.

So we call requests_get with url "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast", headers default, params: latitude=41.0535, longitude=-73.7629, daily=["temperature_2m_max","temperature_2m_min"], temperature_unit="celsius", forecast_days=7, timezone="auto".

But the function signature expects params as an object with keys: latitude, longitude, elevation, etc. It doesn't mention daily, temperature_unit, forecast_days, timezone. But maybe they omitted them. However we can still pass them because the function likely passes through unknown keys. But we need to match the signature exactly. The signature shows only latitude, longitude, elevation. But we can add other keys? The signature says "params:" then a dictionary with keys: latitude, longitude, elevation. But maybe the tool accepts additional keys. Usually the tool will accept any query parameters. So we can pass daily, temperature_unit, forecast_days, timezone. Let's do that.

Thus:

{
"url": "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
"params": {
"latitude": 41.0535,
"longitude": -73.7629,
